To solve the problem of maximizing the cardinality of a set of distinct integers in $2 \dots 256$ such that for every three distinct members $a, b, c$, $a \nmid bc$, we can analyze the divisibility condition.

The condition $a \nmid bc$ for all distinct $a, b, c \in S$ is equivalent to saying that no element $a \in S$ divides the product of any two other distinct elements in $S$.

Let's consider the structure of such a set.
If we include a composite number $a$, it has prime factors. If we include its prime factors, say $p$ and $q$ (where $p, q$ are distinct primes and $a = pq$), then $p \mid a \cdot q$ (since $a \cdot q = p q^2$) and $q \mid a \cdot p$ (since $a \cdot p = p^2 q$). This violates the condition. Thus, we cannot have a composite number and its prime factors all in the set if they are distinct.

A known strategy for such "product-free" or "divisibility-free" type problems on $\{2, \dots, N\}$ is to select numbers that are "large" enough so that their products exceed $N$, or to select numbers with specific prime factor properties.

Consider the set of all integers in $(N/2, N]$.
Let $S = \{ k \in \mathbb{Z} \mid N/2 < k \le N \}$.
If $a, b, c \in S$ are distinct, then $a > N/2, b > N/2, c > N/2$.
Then $bc > N^2/4$.
For $N=256$, $N^2/4 = 16384$.
The maximum element in $S$ is $256$.
Does $a \mid bc$?
If $a \mid bc$, then $bc = k a$ for some integer $k \ge 1$.
Since $a \le N$ and $bc > N^2/4$, we have $k = bc/a > N/4 = 64$.
Also $bc < N^2$, so $k < N = 256$.
